subject: physics
question_text: Why do we have different units for the same physical quantity?

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The reason
lines: One physical quantity can take a very wide
range of magnitudes, so a single unit would
be clumsy at one end of that range.
steps.why: A unit is chosen so the measured number is convenient. Quoting a person’s mass in tonnes or a truck’s mass in milligrams is correct but unusable.
common_mistakes: Saying different countries use different units. The reason asked for is the range of magnitudes.

recall.must_convey: That a quantity covers a wide range of magnitudes, so different units suit different ranges.

steps.memory_tip: The unit is picked so the NUMBER is convenient. Range drives the choice.
steps.margin_note: One reason, then straight to the example.

steps.label: Examples
lines: Each unit keeps the measured number in a
range that is easy to write and read.
steps.why: Giving two different quantities shows the reason is general, not a fact about mass alone. Length itself runs from a nucleus (about 10⁻¹⁵ m, 1 fermi) and an atom (about 10⁻¹⁰ m, 1 ångström) to the earth–sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m, 1 AU). No single unit serves that whole range.
common_mistakes: Giving units of two different quantities, such as metre and kilogram, as if they were alternatives for one quantity.

recall.must_convey: That mass can be measured in milligram, gram, kilogram or tonne, and length in millimetre, metre or kilometre.

steps.memory_tip: Give one ladder of units for ONE quantity, smallest to largest.
steps.margin_note: A ladder of units reads better than a list.

insider_note: This one is in the TSBIE material but not the Fastrack. One reason plus one example is the whole answer.
